Default subverses are the heart of content aggregators and therefore are the front line for any ideological battles that inevitably take place within the community. Due to this, it is of the utmost importance to regulate them in a manner that makes defaults extremely difficult to game.

The most important issue surrounding defaults is, of course, their moderation. We've seen how easy it is for corrupt moderators to censor content and push a narrative that fits their personal politics. Public modlogs have mitigated this problem to an extent, allowing users to audit moderation and speak out against abuse by appealing to an easily accessible body of evidence.

However, in my opinion the system needs further refinement. The users are still beholden to the adminstration to solve mod abuse, and if action isn't taken immediately to resolve the issue, users inevitably fall back on vigilante justice, effectively "assassinating" mods using downvote brigades. This poses as much of a problem for online communities because mobs are easily incited by trolls, autocrats, and their sock puppet armies. There is nothing in place that prevents innocent mods from being the victim of political assassinations. What we need to stem mod abuse is a system of due process in which the users can remove default mods when there is no reasonable doubt of abuse.

Creating a system in such a fashion is more or less impossible on voat in its current state. But we can at very least discuss how we might go about it under more ideal conditions. Here are some of my thoughts on how this might be done:

  • Default moderators should be elected and elections should be held in regular intervals. (We'd need to somehow prevent sockpuppet brigading of elections to make this work.)

  • Modlogs should be audited and users should be made aware of any potential abuses.

  • Rules for default subverses should be as unambiguous and non-arbitrary as possible.

  • Users should have some form of referendum power to change rules on default subverses.

  • In the event of mod abuse, the issue should be discussed openly. The mod in question must be allowed to defend him or herself, and other users should be allowed to advocate on his or her behalf.

  • After discussion, the userbase should be able to call a vote. In order to prevent incitement against an innocent mod, I propose that removal should only occur if 50% of the userbase and 50% of default moderators vote for removal. (Remember, in this system, default mods are your representatives and have to depend upon your votes to continue modding a default sub.)

Now for the most important part: How do you think moderation should be regulated on default subs?
